issues.subcategory: implausible generation slope summary for wheel speed
issues.description: The reported generation effect summary for wheel speed is internally inconsistent with the stated observed means. The manuscript reports a generation effect mean of 5.37 m/h with a 95% CI of (1.58, 9.02), yet the descriptive means increase from 123.6 to 145.7 m/h across five generations, implying a total increase of 22.1 m/h, or roughly 5.5 m/h per generation if coded linearly across four generation steps. However, the quote presents this as 'average wheel speed increased across generations' while simultaneously labeling the interval as 'Generation 95% Confidence Intervals', which is unclear and inconsistent with later Bayesian HPDIs. The parameter meaning, scale, and interval type are not clearly aligned with the descriptive statistics.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations (Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h, Figure 2.A)

issues.subcategory: mixed use of frequentist and Bayesian interval terminology
issues.description: The manuscript states that Bayesian multilevel models were used and that 95% credible intervals were used for inference, but the Results repeatedly report '95% Confidence Intervals' for model parameters and '95% Highest Posterior Density Interval' for descriptive generation estimates. Mixing confidence intervals with Bayesian posterior intervals without explanation is statistically incorrect or at minimum highly misleading. Readers cannot tell whether the reported intervals are Bayesian credible intervals, HPDIs, or frequentist confidence intervals.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: incompatible interval labels in results
issues.description: The Results alternately report '95% Confidence Intervals' and '95% Highest Posterior Density Interval' for quantities arising from the same Bayesian modeling framework, without clarifying which are model coefficients and which are posterior summaries, or how they were computed. This creates ambiguity about the inferential framework and may indicate incorrect reporting of Bayesian outputs as frequentist confidence intervals.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations (Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02)... The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6))

issues.subcategory: inappropriate linear model for bounded count score
issues.description: Understanding score is a bounded discrete count based on 10 forced-choice items, yet the authors modeled it with a linear model. This can violate distributional assumptions and produce misleading uncertainty estimates, especially with ceiling/floor constraints and discrete outcomes. A binomial or ordinal/item-level model would have been more appropriate and would preserve the structure of the task.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable, “Generation” as a predictor variable and “Chain’s identity” as a random effect

issues.subcategory: inappropriate aggregation of item-level understanding measure
issues.description: The understanding outcome aggregates across two distinct 5-item subdomains (moment of inertia and centre of mass), each with potentially different patterns. Aggregating into a single total score after the preregistered model failed to converge changes the estimand and can mask theoretically relevant tradeoffs. The nonconvergence itself suggests the original model specification was problematic, but the chosen remedy is not justified statistically.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: post hoc model change after nonconvergence
issues.description: The authors deviated from the preregistered analysis because the original model did not converge, then switched to an aggregated outcome and removed predictors. This introduces substantial analytic flexibility. There is no reporting of attempts to improve convergence, alternative justified model specifications, prior sensitivity, or whether conclusions were robust across models. Because the change bears directly on one of the main claims about understanding, this is consequential.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: data-restricted analyses differ across preregistered tests
issues.description: The speed analyses restrict data to participants’ last two trials 'in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend', but another analysis assigns failures a speed of 0. These differing handling rules across analyses create researcher degrees of freedom and affect comparability between analyses. Restricting to later trials may inflate apparent optimization by excluding early failures and should be justified in relation to the preregistration.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent handling of failure trials
issues.description: Failure trials are handled inconsistently across analyses: excluded in Analysis 1, assigned speed 0 in Analysis 3, and Figure 2 reports average speed only for non-failure wheels while separately plotting counts of failures. Because failure/non-failure is itself a performance outcome, these analytic choices materially affect results. No rationale is given for why different analyses use different definitions of performance.
issues.quote: Analysis 1 ... Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset... Analysis 3 ... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.subcategory: missing exact coding of generation and trial variables
issues.description: The manuscript does not state how 'Generation' and 'Trial' were coded in the models (e.g., 1-5, centered, standardized), whether random slopes were considered, or the exact model formulas and priors in the main text. This prevents interpretation of coefficient magnitudes such as 5.37 m/h or 0.44 and limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable, “Trial”, “Generation” as predictor variables and “Player’s identity” and “Chain’s identity” as random effects

issues.subcategory: model selection based on fit to observed data
issues.description: The final model was selected after comparing candidate models based on fit to observed data. This is a major source of analytic flexibility, particularly because the preregistration is invoked elsewhere. No criteria are given (e.g., WAIC, LOO, posterior predictive checks), no list of candidate models is presented in the main text, and no model uncertainty is acknowledged.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding in data collection and analysis
issues.description: The experimenter both implemented the wheel configurations and was not blind to condition, and data analyses were also not blind. Since the experimenter physically positioned the weights and released the wheel, lack of blinding could influence setup, handling, or timing-related aspects, especially in a hands-on apparatus experiment. This threatens internal validity.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments... Data analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: experimenter manually implements participant configurations
issues.description: Participants selected configurations via computer, but the experimenter physically placed the weights on the wheel. This introduces room for implementation error or subtle condition-related bias. No inter-rater or setup accuracy checks are reported, nor any verification that the wheel was configured exactly as selected.
issues.quote: Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly

issues.subcategory: underpowered subgroup analyses of inherited theory types
issues.description: The exploratory analyses split participants into inherited-theory categories with very small subgroup sizes, especially the 'full theory' group (N=6). Any visual or inferential conclusions from these subgroups are highly unstable. Yet these analyses support substantive claims about exploration and understanding patterns.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory... 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: no statistical tests reported for exploratory subgroup claims
issues.description: The manuscript describes exploratory subgroup differences in exploration and understanding as 'striking' and 'strongly affected', but does not report model specifications, effect sizes, interval estimates, or uncertainty for these subgroup comparisons in the main text. Without inferential details, readers cannot evaluate the robustness of these central mechanistic claims.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior... Furthermore, inherited theories strongly affected participant's understanding of the wheel system.

issues.subcategory: understanding test may measure forced-choice discrimination not causal understanding
issues.description: The central construct is 'causal understanding', but the operational measure is a 10-item prediction task asking which wheel would descend faster. This primarily assesses comparative prediction accuracy for specific exemplars, not necessarily explicit or mechanistic causal understanding. A participant could learn a heuristic for the presented pair types without understanding the system, while someone with partial understanding could be penalized by the 'No difference' option or item design.
issues.quote: Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.

issues.subcategory: same order of understanding items for all participants
issues.description: All participants received the same 10 pairs in the same order. This invites order effects, fatigue effects, and item-specific learning within the test. Because the measure is used to compare generations and treatments, lack of randomization undermines construct validity and can introduce systematic bias.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous correctness when no-difference option is allowed
issues.description: Participants could answer 'No difference', but the manuscript does not explain how this was scored for each item or whether any pairs were near-equal. Without item-level scoring rules and validation, the interpretation of the understanding score is unclear. This is especially important because chance performance is referenced repeatedly.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

issues.subcategory: missing psychometric properties of understanding measure
issues.description: No reliability, item difficulty, discrimination, or validation data are provided for the 10-item understanding test. Given that understanding is a primary outcome, readers need evidence that the measure is internally consistent and sensitive enough to detect change across generations or treatments.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: causal claims from non-randomized inherited-theory content
issues.description: The manuscript makes causal claims that inheriting an inertia or centre-of-mass theory changes exploration and understanding. However, theory content was not randomized; it emerged endogenously from prior participants. Thus inherited-theory category is confounded with chain history, generation, prior configurations, and participant behavior. The observed associations cannot identify causal effects of theory content.
issues.quote: Inheriting an inertia-related theory increased their understanding of inertia, but decreased their understanding of centre of mass; symmetrically, inheriting a centre-of-mass-related theory increased their understanding of centre of mass, but decreased their understanding about inertia.

issues.subcategory: mechanism claim unsupported by design
issues.description: The manuscript concludes that theory transmission constrained exploration and thereby produced downstream effects on understanding. But because neither exploration strategy nor inherited theory content was experimentally manipulated independently, the proposed mediation pathway remains speculative. Alternative explanations, including selection into particular wheel regions due to inherited configurations or chain-specific norms, are not ruled out.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: overstated conclusion that causal understanding is not necessary
issues.description: The title and core conclusion are broader than what the experiment establishes. The task is a simple, highly constrained optimization problem with social transmission and only five within-person trials. Showing improvement without measured explicit understanding in this task does not establish that causal understanding is unnecessary for improvement of culturally evolving technology in general. At most, it suggests one route to improvement under these laboratory conditions.
issues.quote: Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from WEIRD student sample
issues.description: The sample consists of French university students, yet the discussion draws broad conclusions about humans, traditional technologies, archaeology, and mixed-gender collaborative settings. The sample is narrow in age, education, and cultural background, and the authors themselves note possible roles of western formal education. This substantially limits external validity.
issues.quote: we asked successive ‘cultural generations’ of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system... In any case, our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities

issues.subcategory: unsupported claim about mixed-gender generalization
issues.description: The discussion claims that findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions to mixed-gender collaborative settings, but no mixed-gender chains were studied. This is a direct overreach beyond the design.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: sex-segregated chains without clear rationale or analysis
issues.description: Participants were assigned to exclusively male or exclusively female chains, but the rationale for this design is not explained, and sex effects are not analyzed or controlled in the main models. This design choice may affect transmission dynamics and limits interpretability, especially given the later unsupported claim about mixed-gender generalization.
issues.quote: In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.subcategory: no balance table for randomization across chains/conditions
issues.description: Although assignment to condition and chain is described as random, no information is provided about balance across sex, age, university background, or physics/engineering background across treatments and generations. This makes it impossible to assess whether randomization succeeded.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition of the experiment and one sex-segregated chain.

issues.subcategory: descriptive optimization percentage unclear or incorrect
issues.description: The statement that results indicate 'an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations' is not transparently derived and appears inconsistent with the reported numbers. If maximum possible speed is about 154 m/h and first-generation speed is 123.6 while generation-5 speed is 145.7, the gain relative to the remaining possible improvement is about (145.7-123.6)/(154-123.6)=72.7%, but this needs explicit definition. As written, 'optimization of 71%' is ambiguous and potentially misleading.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: 1 meter track versus 92 cm timed distance
issues.description: The manuscript alternately describes the wheel as traveling down a 1-meter track and reports switches 92 cm apart as the timed start/end points. This discrepancy matters because speed is defined as 1m/descent time in the Results, which is inconsistent with the apparatus description. Speed values may therefore be miscomputed or mislabeled.
issues.quote: The physical system was a wheel that traveled down a 1-meter long inclined track... Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails... The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time)

issues.subcategory: unit inconsistency in speed reporting
issues.description: Reported speeds are in m/h, which are implausible and likely intended to be m/h based on converting short descent times, but the manuscript uses 1 m over fractions of a second. Given the 92 cm timing issue and the unusual use of m/h for a laboratory track, there is substantial ambiguity in the scale and calculation of the outcome variable. This complicates interpretation of effect sizes and payoff calculations.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h

issues.subcategory: missing handling of repeated measures structure in understanding test
issues.description: The understanding measure consists of 10 item responses per participant, but the main analyses collapse these into a score. The manuscript does not report item-level modeling, whether items differed in difficulty, or whether dependence among items was examined. This omission is important because the measure is central and item heterogeneity could mask effects.
issues.quote: After completing the task... participants compared 10 pairs of wheels.

issues.subcategory: performance incentives may distort exploration and theory writing
issues.description: Participants' pay depended on their own wheel performance and the next participant’s first two wheels, and in the theory condition they also wrote theories to be transmitted. These incentives could encourage strategic withholding, vague or misleading theorizing, or optimization specifically of transmissible final trials rather than genuine understanding. This is not discussed as a design limitation.
issues.quote: Participants were informed that their last two trials would be transmitted to the next participant in the chain, and that their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain.

issues.subcategory: main conclusion conflates absence of measured increase with absence of necessity
issues.description: The manuscript infers that because measured understanding did not improve across generations while wheel performance did, causal understanding is not necessary. This is too strong: null change in the chosen understanding measure does not demonstrate lack of relevant understanding, and necessity is not tested by the design. Participants may have used tacit, partial, or nonverbal causal knowledge not captured by the test.
issues.quote: This confirms that the retention of improvements over generations produces highly optimized solutions and need not depend on the emergence of more accurate causal models.

issues.subcategory: theory coding conflates accuracy with presence of keywords
issues.description: The coding scheme classifies theories as inertia-related or centre-of-mass-related if they mention certain qualitative features. This may misclassify partial, vague, or mixed statements, and it is unclear how inaccurate but dimension-relevant statements were handled. Coding 'contains accurate information related to' a principle is not equivalent to measuring the quality or completeness of a causal model.
issues.quote: were asked to code participants’ theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: missing details of candidate models and priors
issues.description: The Bayesian analyses lack key details necessary for evaluation and replication: priors, number of iterations, chains, convergence diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, and the exact candidate models compared. Reliance on a supplement is possible, but the main paper gives insufficient information for the central inferential claims.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33

issues.subcategory: no sample size justification or power analysis
issues.description: The authors explicitly state that no statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size and justify N only by comparison to previous studies. This is not an adequate basis for power, particularly for interaction effects, random-effects models, and small subgroup exploratory analyses. The null conclusions about theory transmission and understanding may therefore reflect low power.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.subcategory: failure trials treated as structural zeros without justification
issues.description: Wheels that did not descend represent a qualitatively different outcome than slow descents. Treating them as speed=0 in one analysis and excluding many such trials in another ignores the missingness/structural nature of these data and can distort model estimates. A two-part or hurdle-type model would better capture descent probability and speed conditional on descent.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.subcategory: no accounting of failure rates by generation/treatment in statistical analyses
issues.description: Figure 2 reportedly shows counts of failures, but the manuscript does not analyze descent failure as an outcome, nor report whether failure rates differed by generation or treatment. Since failures are directly relevant to optimization, omitting formal analysis leaves an incomplete picture of performance change.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment.

issues.subcategory: same experimenter likely responsible for release and apparatus handling
issues.description: The wheel was manually positioned and released via a mechanical system, but no calibration, inter-session reliability, or procedural standardization is reported. Small differences in release setup or wheel placement could affect timings, especially when effect sizes are on the order of seconds or less.
issues.quote: The wheel was then positioned on the rails and held motionless by a mechanical system before being released.

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of cultural niche hypothesis prediction
issues.description: The manuscript states that the cultural niche hypothesis predicts no improvement in understanding across generations. That is stronger than what many formulations imply; cumulative culture can in some cases co-develop with improved understanding, depending on transmission and domain. The framing sets up a dichotomy between explicit causal understanding and cumulative culture that may be overly sharp.
issues.quote: The cultural niche hypothesis predicts that the speed of the wheel will increase with generations, while participants’ understanding of the system will not improve over generations

issues.subcategory: number of generations phrasing inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript refers to chains of 5 individuals and later says optimization occurred 'after only four cultural generations.' This is ambiguous because five individuals imply five generation positions unless generation 1 is treated as baseline and four transitions are counted. The terminology should be clarified to avoid confusion.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals... these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: missing inter-rater aggregation rule for theory coding
issues.description: Although Cohen's kappa is reported for theory coding, the manuscript does not specify how disagreements were resolved, whether majority vote or consensus was used, or whether coders were blind to treatment/generation metadata. This matters because exploratory conclusions depend heavily on these categories.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel... Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters

issues.subcategory: task simplicity limits extrapolation to real technologies
issues.description: The discussion extrapolates from a two-dimensional laboratory wheel task to complex, high-dimensional cultural technologies such as bows, kayaks, and archaeological artifacts. The authors note the task is a conservative test, but the simplification also drastically reduces demands of real-world technology development, social learning, materials constraints, and functional tradeoffs.
issues.quote: Finally, although the physics of the system are by no means trivial, the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses, compared to the many-dimensional problem of optimizing, for example, the performance of a bow

issues.subcategory: confounding by inherited configurations in theory-treatment comparisons
issues.description: In the Configurations + Theory treatment, participants inherit both configurations and theories. Any effect attributed to theory transmission is confounded by the content of inherited configurations, which themselves differ across chains and may correlate with theory content. The design lacks a condition isolating theory transmission from configuration transmission.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.subcategory: absence of control condition without social transmission
issues.description: The study tests cumulative improvement across generations with social transmission, but lacks an asocial control or individual-learning baseline spanning equivalent total trial numbers. Without such a control, it is difficult to quantify how much improvement reflects cumulative cultural transmission versus within-person task affordances or general optimization under repeated attempts.
issues.quote: All participants except those in the first generation were provided with social information.

issues.subcategory: insufficient detail on preregistration adherence
issues.description: Although the study is preregistered, the manuscript only briefly notes one deviation. It does not systematically indicate which analyses, exclusions, transformations, and exploratory components were preregistered versus post hoc. Given the multiple analyses and changes, clearer demarcation is needed.
issues.quote: The study was pre-registered (https://osf.io/ge7cs). Pre-registration of the study design, hypotheses and analysis plan took place before any data were collected.
